sections.h2: How can a Harrison owner sell quickly?
sections.html:
Harrison owners can list through an agent, sell privately, or accept an as-is cash purchase, and only the last avoids staging, showings and renovation deadlines. With the Census median home value above $1 million, a rushed sale can cost a great deal, so weigh any offer against what similar Harrison houses have sold for.

Harrison is a combined town and village in Westchester County, about 27 miles from Grand Central. That setup creates local wrinkles for sellers: one building department for the whole municipality, a Receiver of Taxes who collects five times a year, and a county clerk who records the deed.

  • Agent listing: works for a house that is ready for the market and an owner with time to spare.
  • Private sale: saves commission but puts negotiation and paperwork on you.
  • Cash purchase: for estates, unfinished projects, tenant-occupied homes or a fixed deadline.

sections.h2: How expensive is housing in Harrison, by the Census?
sections.html:
QuickFacts shows 32,273 people in Harrison as of July 2025, against 28,218 counted in 2020. Owner-occupied homes carry a median value of $1,010,700 for 2020 to 2024, and 60.5% of homes are owned by their occupants.

Rents are high too, at a median $2,616 a month. Median household income reaches $164,250 in 2024 dollars across 9,222 households averaging 2.88 people, and 60.4% of adults have at least a bachelor's degree. The mean trip to work is 29.2 minutes. Because the median value sits just over $1 million, a large share of Harrison sales reach the level where New York's 1% mansion tax, paid by the buyer, applies.

Land area is 16.77 square miles, which gives about 1,683 residents per square mile at the 2020 count.

sections.h2: How is Harrison arranged, and what does each area offer a buyer?
sections.html:
Harrison is shaped roughly like a figure eight, with downtown Harrison in the south and the hamlets of Purchase and West Harrison to the north. Founded under a patent in 1696 and made a town in 1788, it became a combined town and village in 1975.

Downtown divides into four sections: Brentwood Plaza, Sunny Ridge, Sterling Ridge/The Trails and the Village part of Harrison, with Halstead Avenue as its main street. West Harrison, around Lake Street and Silver Lake Park, has few road entrances. Purchase holds Manhattanville University, SUNY Purchase and, through its corporate campuses along I-287, the area known as the Platinum Mile. Harrison station on Metro-North's New Haven Line is the commuter link, and Westchester County Airport lies almost entirely within Purchase.

Much of the older housing dates from the 1920s through the 1950s. The Sunny Ridge subdivision was laid out on a former farm after 1929, and most of its houses went up from the mid-1940s on, in colonial revival and Tudor styles. Sites on the National Register include the Hadden-Margolis House, built around 1750, and the 1938 Post Office. Owners of period homes should keep records of past renovations, since buyers of older houses ask for them.

  • Roads: I-95, I-287, I-684 and the Hutchinson River Parkway, plus NY 120, 120A and 127.
  • Bus: the Bee-Line system.
  • Employers: corporate headquarters including MasterCard and PepsiCo.

The Harrison Central School District runs Harrison High School and Louis M. Klein Middle School, both downtown, plus four elementary schools. Purchase School covers Purchase and the north of West Harrison, Preston covers the Silver Lake area, Parsons covers south downtown, and Harrison Avenue School covers the rest of downtown.

Elementary attendance zones follow neighborhoods, so an address in Sunny Ridge and one in Purchase feed different schools. Higher education is nearby as well: Manhattanville University and SUNY Purchase are in Purchase, and Fordham opened a Westchester campus in West Harrison in 2008. Keio Academy of New York, a private high school, is also in Purchase.

sections.h2: How does Harrison assess and collect property tax?
sections.html:
The Assessor's Office maintains a record card for each of roughly 7,000 parcels and values them on current sales and cost, then applies the tax rate to produce each bill. The Receiver of Taxes collects town, village, school, county and state tax from a single office in the Municipal Building.

Harrison assessment and tax calendar (source: Town/Village of Harrison Assessor and Receiver of Taxes)
DateEvent
May 1Taxable status date; exemptions due
June 1Tentative roll filed; grievance period opens
Third Tuesday in JuneGrievance period ends
September 15Final roll filed
February and JuneTown and village tax due
January and SeptemberSchool tax due
AprilCounty and state tax due

Bills are mailed before the first of the month and must be paid by the month's last day, though mailing them is a courtesy and a lost bill does not excuse a late payment. The town says roughly 56% of collections go to schools, 25% to the town and 19% to the county. Changes of ownership should be reported to the tax office in writing.

sections.h2: What permits does Harrison require, and why do they matter at sale?
sections.html:
Harrison requires a building permit for new buildings, additions, alterations and accessory structures, and the Building Inspector issues the Certificate of Occupancy. A buyer's attorney will look for both on any house with visible improvements.

Most residential construction needs Architectural Board of Review approval, and permits cover sheds, decks, pools, interior alterations, fences, driveways, tree removal, plumbing and electrical work. The department may ask for a final as-built survey after new construction, additions, accessory structures, fences, walls or altered driveways. The Assessor learns of completed work from the permit and inspects with the Building Inspector, then adjusts the assessment, so unpermitted additions can surface as both a code problem and a higher bill.

  • Collect permits and Certificates of Occupancy for each improvement.
  • Find the most recent survey; the department wants 36 by 48 inches at standard size.
  • Counter hours run 9am to 5pm, and applications go in person or by mail rather than electronically.

sections.h2: What does recording a deed in Westchester cost?
sections.html:
The Westchester County Clerk's Land Records Division records Harrison deeds. Its fee schedule lists a $45 statutory fee, $5 per written page, $5 for the TP-584 form on residential property and $125 for the RP-5217 transfer report, so a three-page residential deed in one municipality costs $190.

New York's transfer tax is $2 for each $500 of price, rounded up, and the clerk's own example turns a $404,501 sale into $1,620. At Harrison's $1,010,700 median value the same calculation gives $4,044. The seller normally pays it; the 1% mansion tax at $1 million or more falls on the buyer. The clerk steers filers to its PREP portal to work out the fees due.

faqs.q: Does Harrison have separate town and village taxes?
faqs.a: Harrison is one combined town and village, and the Receiver of Taxes collects both, with payments due in February and June. School tax is billed separately for January and September, and county and state tax in April.

faqs.q: When can a Harrison owner contest an assessment?
faqs.a: The grievance period runs from June 1, when the tentative roll is filed, to the third Tuesday in June. The Assessor sets May 1 as the date exemptions are due, and the final roll is filed September 15.

faqs.q: Is a permit needed for a deck or shed in Harrison?
faqs.a: Yes. Sheds, decks, pools and interior alterations all need permits, and most residential construction also needs Architectural Board of Review approval. The Building Inspector issues the Certificate of Occupancy.

faqs.q: What does the buyer pay on a million-dollar Harrison sale?
faqs.a: A 1% mansion tax applies when a residence sells for $1 million or more, and the buyer pays it. The seller covers New York's base transfer tax of $2 per $500, paid at recording.

faqs.q: Where is a Harrison deed filed?
faqs.a: With the Westchester County Clerk's Land Records Division. A recording needs the deed, form TP-584, form RP-5217 and the filing fees, which the clerk's PREP portal can calculate.
